t: Human in the loop, or human rubber stamp?
s: Last week, Lord Sales, Deputy President of the UK Supreme Court, said something most judges avoid saying out loud: AI could one day decide some court cases.
x: human in the loop, or human rubber stamp? last week, lord sales, deputy president of the uk supreme court, said something most judges avoid saying out loud: ai could one day decide some court cases. "for low-value civil disputes, we may eventually accept forms of automated determination, particularly where parties agree." his reason is practical. courts are facing a "tsunami" of claims written and filed with ai, and he thinks courts may have to use ai to cope. but the more important part of his speech was a warning: "the 'human in the loop' can gradually become the human rubber stamp." he calls it automation bias: "the tendency to accept the machine's answer precisely because the machine usually gets things right." the long-term danger, he said, is that people "gradually lose the ability to know whether it has got the answer wrong." he also asked a question every law firm should answer. if ai does the research and first drafts that juniors used to do, "where does the experienced senior lawyer come from?" in his words, the slower human process was producing "today's legal work and tomorrow's lawyer." india has drawn a harder line: → july 2025: the kerala high court's ai policy bars district courts from using ai to arrive at findings, reliefs, orders or judgments. → june 2026: the supreme court's ai committee published draft regulations for use of ai in courts, 2026, proposing a complete ban on ai deciding judicial outcomes, built on "human primacy". lawyers would have to disclose ai-assisted filings. → the cji has said ai can help with research and managing work, but judgment must stay with judges. i think india is right to keep ai out of deciding cases for now. but a ban on ai verdicts does not solve the quieter problem lord sales describes. that problem sits with us: lawyers who accept a polished draft because it is usually right. for young lawyers like me, a few habits help: 1. do some work the slow way. draft a few pleadings and research notes yourself. 2. read ai output like the other side's draft. look for what is wrong, missing or invented. 3. verify every citation and quotation against the official report. 4. expect to disclose ai use. the draft rules would require it. speed is useful. judgment is the job. would you accept an ai decision in a small claim if both sides agreed? i'd like to hear from lawyers and non-lawyers. the full breakdown is in the slides. views are personal and for general information only; not legal advice. artificialintelligence aiincourts legaltech ruleoflaw judicialreform t: Can a rival buy your brand name on Amazon?
s: Kent RO has sued Amazon in the Delhi High Court (CS(COMM) 1145/2026). It alleges that its well-known mark "KENT" is sold as an advertising keyword, so shoppers searching for Kent purifiers…
x: can a rival buy your brand name on amazon? kent ro has sued amazon in the delhi high court cs comm 1145/2026 . it alleges that its well-known mark "kent" is sold as an advertising keyword, so shoppers searching for kent purifiers see competing products first. 🔎 how keyword ads work a seller bids on "kent". a shopper searches "kent". a rival's product appears at the top, marked "sponsored". the platform earns on every click. the word "kent" may never appear in the ad, which courts call "invisible use". 📅 where the case stands • justice tejas karia issued summons on 16 october; amazon has accepted notice. • kent placed a video on record showing the keyword bidding process. • no interim relief yet. the application will be heard on 8 december. ⚖️ the law the court will apply 1️⃣ google v. drs logistics division bench, 2023 : using a mark as a keyword is "use" in advertising even if it's never shown, but it isn't infringement per se. there must be confusion, unfair advantage or dilution. google got no safe harbour because it actively promoted trademarks as keywords. 2️⃣ hindware v. grohe may 2026 : invisible keyword use is use; google "was not neutral but an active commercial participant". google has appealed. ❓ three questions for a marketplace • who is using the mark: the seller who bids, or the platform that runs the auction and earns from it? • is there confusion? the shopper is already inside the store and the ad says "sponsored", but kent is a well-known mark, which gets wider protection. • is amazon a passive intermediary? after drs and hindware, the search engine that sold keywords didn't get safe harbour. amazon will have to show its role is different. ✅ what this means now • brands: search your own name on marketplaces and keep a record of what appears. • sellers: bidding on a rival's well-known mark is a real litigation risk; generic terms are safer. • platforms: "we're just an intermediary" is harder to argue. my take: keyword ads aren't wrong in themselves. they're lawful unless they confuse buyers or take unfair advantage of a mark's reputation. for a well-known mark like kent, on a platform that profits from every click, that line is easier to cross. 📎 resources: • livelaw biz: https://www.livelawbiz.com/trademark/kent-ro-moves-delhi-high-court-against-amazon-over-use-of-kent-as-advertising-keyword-558881 • google v. drs judgment : https://spicyip.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/google-v.-drs.pdf • mondaq on hindware: https://www.mondaq.com/india/trademark/1822848/when-does-keyword-use-become-trademark-infringement when you search a brand and see a rival's product first, do you feel misled, or is it just shopping? views are personal; for general information only. suit pending; no interim order yet. trademarklaw keywordadvertising ecommerce delhihighcourt intellectualproperty amazon digitalmarketing intermediaryliability legalupdate

t: Personality rights aren't only for celebrities
s: On 16 November, the Madras High Court restrained Blinkit from using the persona of Saravanan Hari, the Chennai Super Kings superfan, without his written consent.
x: personality rights aren't only for celebrities on 16 november, the madras high court restrained blinkit from using the persona of saravanan hari, the chennai super kings superfan, without his written consent. 📰 the facts • since around 2013, hari has appeared at csk matches with a yellow-painted face, curly wig, moustache, dhoni's no. 7 and a thumbs-up pose. it is widely covered on tv. • on 23 march 2025, a blinkit ad on the front page of the sunday times showed a cartoon figure with the same look and pose. • people he knew asked whether he was endorsing blinkit. pre-suit mediation failed, and he sued, claiming ₹1.1 crore. ⚖️ blinkit's defence: the characters were fictional and didn't resemble him. the court found a clear resemblance: the same pose was reproduced, and the public was likely to be misled into thinking it was him. 💬 the key line justice p.b. balaji : "the constitution protects the rights of every individual and it need not be restricted or limited to celebrities like actors and sportspersons." blinkit could not exploit his personality rights, "whatever little it may be", for commercial gain without consent. 📌 relief interim : no commercial use without written consent; the ad's artwork and emails must be preserved. the publisher's liability will be decided at trial. next hearing: 14 december. 🧭 where this fits in t. rangaraj january 2026 , the madras high court refused takedowns where posts merely circulated, insisting on commercial exploitation. hari's case applies the same test to a non-celebrity. read together, the test is identifiability plus commercial use without consent, not fame. 🔐 the privacy-law gap why not the dpdp act? section 3 c ii excludes personal data that the person made publicly available, and a fan appearing on tv at matches may fall within that exclusion. most of the act also only applies from 13 may 2027. personality rights and passing off fill that gap. ✅ for brands and agencies 1️⃣ get written consent for any recognisable person, even as a cartoon or look-alike. 2️⃣ don't recreate a known pose or signature look. 3️⃣ ai-generated look-alikes carry the same risk. my take: if people recognise you, a brand needs your permission. that protects ordinary people without turning the right into a tool to silence fans, critics or the news. 📎 resources: • livelaw biz: https://www.livelawbiz.com/personality-rights/madras-high-court-protects-csk-fan-personality-rights-restraining-blinkit-from-using-image-without-consent-558695 • spicyip on t. rangaraj: https://spicyip.com/2026/01/a-course-correction-what-rangaraj-and-kamal-haasan-get-right-about-personality-rights.html should a local "famous face" have the same rights as a film star when a brand copies them? t: AI training and copyright: three courts, three answers
s: In ten days, courts in Europe, Canada and the US each moved on the same question: can an AI company train on copyrighted work without permission?
x: ai training and copyright: three courts, three answers in ten days, courts in europe, canada and the us each moved on the same question: can an ai company train on copyrighted work without permission? 🇪🇺 european union 3 november in like company v. google c-250/25 , advocate general szpunar said training is "as a rule, freely permitted" under the text-and-data-mining exception, if developers: • use only lawfully accessible sources • respect machine-readable opt-outs such as robots.txt • take steps to stop the model reproducing specific works but a chatbot fetching and reusing news in real time may still infringe press publishers' rights. 🇨🇦 canada 13 november the ontario court of appeal unanimously held that openai must defend the canadian news publishers' suit in ontario. openai argued that its training happened outside the province. the court found "a real and substantial connection". canadian fair dealing, not us fair use, will apply, and there is no text-and-data-mining exception. this decides venue only. 🇺🇸 united states pending in in re openai copyright infringement litigation, judge sidney stein will decide fair use on cross-motions for summary judgment, without a trial. on 6 november he allowed 56 amicus briefs. 🇮🇳 and india? in ani v. openai, the delhi high court 24 july kept jurisdiction, held training-related storage prima facie covered by section 52 1 a i , and refused an interim injunction. ani's appeal is pending. indonesia is legislating instead, and google, meta and tiktok opposed its bill on 11 november. three patterns across the courts: 1️⃣ location isn't a shield. delhi and ontario both rejected "we trained abroad". 2️⃣ opt-outs matter. the eu makes them the line, and the delhi hc weighed the unused crawler opt-out against ani. 3️⃣ outputs are the weak point. regurgitation is where liability sits. my take: india shouldn't leave this to one interim order. stretching "private use, including research" to cover commercial ai training is a fragile base for a whole industry. a clear statutory rule with opt-outs, transparency and anti-memorisation duties would serve creators and developers better. 📎 resources: • cjeu press release: https://curia.europa.eu/site/jcms/p1 1000088855 • ctv on ontario: https://ctvnews.ca/sci-tech/article/court-allows-news-publishers-copyright-lawsuit-against-openai-to-go-ahead • ipwatchdog on the us briefs: https://ipwatchdog.com/2026/11/02/openai-touts-briefs-backing-fair-use-for-ai-training/ • livelaw on ani: https://www.livelaw.in/high-court/delhi-high-court/delhi-high-court-rejects-ani-copyright-suit-open-ai-chatgpt-542736 which approach should india take: fair dealing, an opt-out exception, or licensing? t: Hyderabad Police now has an AI that maps "criminal networks". Which law tells it where to stop?
s: On 12 November, Commissioner V.C. Sajjanar launched Dooradrishti, an AI platform built in-house by Hyderabad City Police. It compiles profiles of accused persons, analyses their activities…
x: hyderabad police now has an ai that maps "criminal networks". which law tells it where to stop? on 12 november, commissioner v.c. sajjanar launched dooradrishti, an ai platform built in-house by hyderabad city police. it compiles profiles of accused persons, analyses their activities and identifies links between individuals and criminal networks, using police databases and data from other departments. the stated aim: faster evidence, faster charge sheets, and a shift "from reactive to proactive policing". organised crime and cyber fraud do run through networks, so the aim is legitimate. but five questions haven't been answered publicly: 1️⃣ does it include people never convicted, or acquitted? 2️⃣ how does it make links, and how are false links caught? 3️⃣ does it reach beyond criminal records, to movements or activity? 4️⃣ who can access it, for how long, and is it audited? 5️⃣ must officers verify its findings before acting? the legal frame: 🔹 puttaswamy: state intrusion on privacy needs a law, a legitimate aim, proportionality and safeguards 🔹 dpdp act s. 17: processing to prevent, detect or investigate offences is largely exempt from may 2027 🔹 malak singh 1981 : police surveillance registers must be limited to people reasonably suspected 🔹 criminal procedure identification act, 2022: records of people never convicted must be destroyed on release, discharge or acquittal and telangana has been here before. in 2022, the high court issued notice in s.q. masood's pil, india's first court challenge to police facial recognition without a law. the risk with network mapping is guilt by link: a relative, neighbour or client flagged by association, old firs and acquittals that never leave the system, and no way to know or correct your profile. being linked to someone isn't evidence of a crime. my take: six safeguards before scale slide 7 : ✔ a published legal basis and sop ✔ scope limited to charge-sheeted and convicted persons, for specific cases ✔ human verification: ai output is a lead, never evidence on its own ✔ deletion for the acquitted and discharged ✔ logs and independent audits of every search ✔ a right to know and correct one's profile, with an annual transparency report hyderabad can lead on ai policing. it should also lead on the rules. 📎 resources: • medianama: https://lnkd.in/d-ichntj • newsmeter: https://lnkd.in/dzfxf2uc what safeguard would you want first? s: Last month I wrote about the news publishers' challenge to the DPDP Act. But the larger case, Venkatesh Nayak v. Union of India, goes well beyond journalism. RTI activist Venkatesh Nayak…
x: can a privacy law quietly weaken the right to information? the supreme court hears that question again on 17 november. last month i wrote about the news publishers' challenge to the dpdp act. but the larger case, venkatesh nayak v. union of india, goes well beyond journalism. rti activist venkatesh nayak, ncpri, the reporters' collective and nitin sethi filed in february. the court issued notice, refused an interim stay and referred the matter to a larger bench. the publishers' plea dnpa joined in october. the central challenge is s. 44 3 , which rewrote rti s. 8 1 j : 🔹 before: personal information was exempt only if unrelated to public activity or an unwarranted invasion of privacy, and could be disclosed if a larger public interest justified it 🔹 after: "information which relates to personal information" is exempt, full stop 🔹 the clause's own public-interest test is gone, and so is the proviso that what can't be denied to parliament can't be denied to a citizen why rti users worry: officials' assets and qualifications, welfare beneficiary lists used in social audits, contractor payments and recruitment records can all now be refused as "personal information". five more provisions are under challenge: 1️⃣ s. 17: wide exemptions for state agencies 2️⃣ s. 36 with rule 23 2 : the centre can demand data from any fiduciary, and the person may not be told 3️⃣ s. 18 with rule 17: board members chosen by an executive-led committee 4️⃣ s. 33 1 : penalties for a "significant" breach, a term the act doesn't define 5️⃣ no journalism exemption the publishers' plea both sides have a case. petitioners call it a "sledgehammer" where a "chisel" was needed, relying on subhash chandra agarwal 2019 . defenders point to puttaswamy, to rti misuse in private disputes, and to s. 8 2 , which still allows disclosure where public interest outweighs harm. the cji said "some ironing out of the creases" might be needed. my take: privacy and transparency aren't opposites. restore a public-interest test inside s. 8 1 j , at least for public functionaries, and bring back the parliament proviso. put independent oversight on s. 36 demands, and make the board truly independent. what to watch on 17 november: the union's reply, whether a larger bench is constituted, and a timeline before may 2027, when most of the act's duties begin. 📎 resources: • supreme court t: Your phone holds your chats, photos, bank apps, health records and contacts. Who can unlock it and copy everything, and under what law?
s: Documents made public by the Internet Freedom Foundation on 10 November show the Home Minister approved a ₹4.98 crore Cellebrite tool for the NIA in January, with a one-time exemption from…
x: your phone holds your chats, photos, bank apps, health records and contacts. who can unlock it and copy everything, and under what law? documents made public by the internet freedom foundation on 10 november show the home minister approved a ₹4.98 crore cellebrite tool for the nia in january, with a one-time exemption from "make in india" procurement rules. the specification: full extraction from android phones and iphones, including encrypted devices, with brute-force passcode attempts. it's not just the nia. iff counts 15 listings naming cellebrite products in 2026 government tenders, from sfio and kerala's home department to karnataka police. delhi police has had such tools since at least 2020. purchase records show procurement, not confirmed use on anyone. the legal gap: 🔹 bnss ss. 105–106 cover search, seizure and video recording, not unlocking or copying a phone 🔹 it act s. 69 needs a written home secretary order to decrypt, and has been under challenge in the supreme court since 2019 🔹 bsa s. 63 certifies electronic records for court; it doesn't make the extraction lawful 🔹 dpdp act s. 17 exempts processing for investigation from may 2027 🔹 guidelines on seizing digital devices, promised to the supreme court in 2023, still haven't been placed before it under puttaswamy, any intrusion on privacy needs a law, a legitimate aim and proportionality. investigating crime is a legitimate aim. but there's no specific law, and full extraction copies far more than any offence needs. if your phone is seized slide 6 : ✔ get the seizure memo listing the device ✔ ask that the hash value be recorded at seizure ✔ take legal advice before giving passwords; the law on compelled passwords is unsettled ✔ lawyers and journalists: flag privileged and source material in writing ✔ apply for return of the device bnss s. 497 and deletion of copied data if you're not charged my take: investigators need these tools, but the rules should come before the purchase orders. a judicial warrant for extraction, scope limited to the offence, a log of every extraction, deletion when no charge is filed, independent audits, and extra protection for lawyers and journalists. 📎 resources: • medianama: https://lnkd.in/dmhvsfwf • internet freedom foundation: https://lnkd.in/damuxmxy should police need a judge's warrant before copying your phone? views are personal; t: Three weeks ago I wrote about courts protecting actors from AI deepfakes. Now the Delhi High Court has given "personality rights" a reality check.
s: In Kriti Sanon v. BBE Marketing Inc & Ors, Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav protected the actor, for now, against AI chatbots and voice models posing as her, sexual deepfakes and…
x: three weeks ago i wrote about courts protecting actors from ai deepfakes. now the delhi high court has given "personality rights" a reality check. in kriti sanon v. bbe marketing inc & ors, justice purushaindra kumar kaurav protected the actor, for now, against ai chatbots and voice models posing as her, sexual deepfakes and impersonating accounts. satire, parody, reviews and fan content are expressly carved out. the reasoning is what matters: 🔹 "personality rights" is an umbrella, not a single cause of action. it covers publicity, passing off, privacy, defamation, and trade mark or copyright rights, including performers' rights 🔹 each claim keeps its own test. bundling them doesn't lower the bar, especially for restraining speech before trial 🔹 mere use of someone's identity isn't unlawful by itself 🔹 "the rights are available to every individual." fame affects only commercial value and loss so plaintiffs must now show which claim, against which defendant, for which content, rather than seeking one blanket injunction. the same week, the same judge decreed amitabh bachchan's suit 5 november , extending it to unknown infringers because the plaint proved a continuing pattern of anonymous misuse. wide relief is still possible when the evidence supports it. if it happens to you slide 6 : ✔ morphed or sexual deepfake: report to the platform, which must remove it within 2 hours under the it rules 2026, and file at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930 ✔ fake account posing as you: platform impersonation report; t: A cartoon exaggerates. A deepfake convinces. Where does political satire end?
s: The Delhi High Court gave an early answer on 6 November in Rekha Gupta v. Aam Aadmi Party & Ors. (Justice Manoj Jain). The Delhi Chief Minister sued over AI-generated videos and images…
x: a cartoon exaggerates. a deepfake convinces. where does political satire end? the delhi high court gave an early answer on 6 november in rekha gupta v. aam aadmi party & ors. justice manoj jain . the delhi chief minister sued over ai-generated videos and images posted from the party's verified accounts, allegedly showing her as a liquor vendor serving drinks and as head of a "ghar ghar theka" scheme. the court described the visuals as a "near-perfect imitation." what the court said: 🔹 public figures must accept criticism and political humour, and parties remain free to attack government policies 🔹 but there is a "thin line": satire "cannot be permitted to create irreparable wound on someone's dignity" 🔹 ai makes realistic fakes easy, but responsibility for making and posting them stays with humans 🔹 content that spreads fast on social media risks irreparable harm it ordered six urls taken down immediately and listed the case for 4 december. this is an interim order; the defendants' case is yet to be heard. why ai changes the satire question: satire works because the audience knows it isn't real. a cartoon or mimicry is obviously exaggeration. a realistic ai video can pass as real, and once shared without context, the joke disappears and only the false impression remains. the legal frame: article 19 1 a protects satire; article 19 2 permits restrictions for defamation. civil suits, criminal defamation bns s. 356 , the february 2026 it rules on labelling synthetic content, and election commission advisories on deepfakes all apply. my take, a five-question test: 1️⃣ would a reasonable viewer know it isn't real? 2️⃣ is it clearly labelled as ai-generated or parody, on the content itself? 3️⃣ does it target a policy, or fabricate conduct by a person? 4️⃣ who posted it? an official party account carries more responsibility 5️⃣ would it be acceptable as a cartoon? if only the realism makes it hurt, the realism is the problem for every party, campaigner and creator slide 7 : label ai content visibly, avoid realistic fabricated acts by real people, aim at policies, and act on takedown requests promptly. if you're targeted: save urls and screenshots, report under the it rules, send a legal notice and seek urgent interim relief. the same rules apply whichever party is in power. 📎 resources: • livelaw on the order: https://lnkd.in/dkigwm2b • bar & bench: https://lnkd.in/dqav-ryd where would you draw the line between ai satire and a deepfake? t: Justice is supposed to be blind. So why do so many case papers still begin with a litigant's caste?
s: In Shama Sharma v. Kishan Kumar (order dated 10 January 2024), the Supreme Court (Justices Hima Kohli and Ahsanuddin Amanullah) directed that the caste or religion of litigants must not…
x: justice is supposed to be blind. so why do so many case papers still begin with a litigant's caste? in shama sharma v. kishan kumar order dated 10 january 2024 , the supreme court justices hima kohli and ahsanuddin amanullah directed that the caste or religion of litigants must not appear in the memo of parties, in the supreme court, in every high court and in every subordinate court. even if the lower court's papers carried it. in the court's words, the practice "is to be shunned and must be ceased forthwith." high courts issued circulars to follow it. in 2025, the allahabad high court went further and barred caste of accused and witnesses in firs and police records, which uttar pradesh implemented, except for sc/st act cases. yet the habit lingers in filings across the country. my take: a caste label on the first page of a case does real damage. 1️⃣ it erodes the image of an unbiased system. a court that labels litigants by caste signals that identity matters, even when it doesn't 2️⃣ it invites bias. identity is on the page before the facts are, and prejudice, conscious or not, can follow 3️⃣ it can be used against marginalised litigants, turning a legal dispute into a social one 4️⃣ it disrupts the process. arguments drift from merits to identity the balance: where caste is the legal issue, such as offences under the sc/st prevention of atrocities act or reservation and caste-certificate disputes, it belongs in the pleadings as a fact, argued on evidence. the rule is about how a litigant is identified, not about hiding relevant facts. for advocates slide 6 : ✔ drop caste and religion from the memo of parties, even if the lower court had them ✔ name, parentage, age, occupation and address are enough to identify a party ✔ plead caste only where it's an ingredient of the case ✔ if the registry objects, cite shama sharma and your high court's circular a litigant is a party, not a caste. equality before law under article 14 starts with the first page of the case. 📎 resources: • livelaw on the judgment: https://lnkd.in/d5dgisek • allahabad hc and up on caste in firs: https://lnkd.in/dvxu3tw3 do you still see caste in case papers in your t: Can Parliament ban a game of skill just because it's played for money? The Supreme Court will decide.
s: India's Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 bans all online money games, whether of chance, skill or both. With its Rules, it took full effect on 1 May 2026:
x: can parliament ban a game of skill just because it's played for money? the supreme court will decide. india's promotion and regulation of online gaming act, 2025 bans all online money games, whether of chance, skill or both. with its rules, it took full effect on 1 may 2026: 🔹 offering or facilitating money games: up to 3 years and/or ₹1 crore fine 3–5 years and up to ₹2 crore for repeat offences 🔹 advertising them: up to 2 years and/or ₹50 lakh 🔹 banks and payment systems can't process them; sites can be blocked under the it act 🔹 e-sports and online social games are allowed, and e-sports will be registered 🔹 a new online gaming authority decides what counts as a money game: stakes, expected winnings, revenue model, and whether rewards can be cashed out the government says around 45 crore people were affected by money gaming, with losses above ₹20,000 crore. the challenge head digital works v. union of india and connected cases : the supreme court moved the high court cases to itself in 2025. on 5 august 2026, a bench led by cji surya kant agreed to a final hearing and asked parties to complete pleadings. there's no interim stay, so the law applies. three questions for the court: 1️⃣ competence: is this "betting and gambling", a state subject, or within parliament's powers? 2️⃣ article 19 1 g : since chamarbaugwala 1957 and k.r. lakshmanan 1996 , games of substantial skill have been treated as legitimate business. can parliament still ban them? 3️⃣ proportionality: is a total ban justified when kyc, deposit limits and age checks exist? s: The EU's "Digital Omnibus" on AI, published in July, delayed the high-risk rules to 2027–28. But it added a new prohibited practice under Article 5 of the AI Act, and it applies in four…

s: The Allahabad High Court has given a clear answer in principle. In Yogendra Maurya v. State of U.P. (order dated 26 October, reported 2 November), Justices Ajit Kumar and Garima Prashad…

x: a "digital arrest" victim sends the money themselves. until now, that meant the bank could say: not our problem. the supreme court has just changed that conversation. on 29 october, a bench of cji surya kant, justice joymalya bagchi and justice v. mohana, hearing the suo motu case on digital arrest scams, told the rbi that its new rules must include a liability clause: 🔹 banks must compensate victims where inadequate safeguards or a failure of due diligence contributed to the fraud 🔹 compensation of not less than the amount the customer lost 🔹 the bank pays, not just the employee involved "the bank will have to pay," said the cji 🔹 safeguards to consider: temporarily holding transactions out of line with an account's history, automatic alerts to police, and verification before release why this matters: the rbi's 2017 circular gives zero liability for "unauthorised" transactions where the bank is at fault. but in a digital arrest, the victim authorises the transfer, under fear and deception. so victims have often fallen outside it, even when the bank let sudden, unusual transfers through without a single check. what's next: the rbi has proposed notifying its kyc amendment directions by 30 november also the next hearing and bringing them into force by 31 december. separately, a draft would let banks flag and hold suspected mule-account transactions, and the government has proposed a one-hour delay on payments of ₹10,000 or more. my take: five questions the final rules must answer. 1️⃣ who decides that due diligence failed? not the bank alone; the burden should stay on the bank, as in 2017 2️⃣ what counts as due diligence? clear triggers: large first-time transfers, new payees, elderly or dormant accounts 3️⃣ how fast is the refund? a provisional credit within days, not years of litigation 4️⃣ who is covered? nbfcs, wallets and payment apps too 5️⃣ what about genuine payments? holds need short time limits and a quick release route if you get the call: no indian agency arrests anyone over a video call, and no genuine officer asks you to transfer money to "verify" it. if you've already paid, call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in immediately, tell your bank in writing, file an fir, and escalate to the rbi ombudsman if needed slide 7 . please share this with your parents and grandparents. they're the most frequent targets. 📎 resources: • business standard: https://lnkd.in/dcvh2qjq • medianama: https://lnkd.in/d7btemea • report cyber fraud: https://cybercrime.gov.in should banks bear the loss when their systems miss an obvious red flag? t: A creator's posts were taken down over copyright complaints. Then his whole Instagram account was suspended. No notice, no hearing. The High Court says that's within the rules.

t: Your page is blocked. You don't know who ordered it, or why. How do you challenge that?
s: Two High Courts dealt with exactly this in the past week.
x: your page is blocked. you don't know who ordered it, or why. how do you challenge that? two high courts dealt with exactly this in the past week. 🔹 punjab & haryana hc haryana 24 news network v. union of india, reported 20 october : a superintendent of police sent meta a notice under section 79 3 b of the it act, and a news company's facebook page was blocked. justice tribhuvan dahiya held: • the notice was without jurisdiction: rule 3 1 d requires an officer of at least dig rank, specifically authorised • when a notice goes to the platform, a copy must go to the user too • the user needn't first use meta's grievance process; without the grounds, there's nothing to answer the page was ordered restored within 24 hours. 🔹 kerala hc hyder ali k. v. union of india, 26 october : malayalam news outlet nocap's facebook page was restricted on 28 september after a "government notice" it has never seen. the court asked the centre and the state whether any order was sent to meta, and listed the case for 5 november. why this keeps happening: section 69a and the 2009 blocking rules give the originator notice and a hearing where possible. that's why shreya singhal upheld them. but many takedowns now go through section 79 3 b : a notice to the platform, which loses safe harbour if it doesn't comply. the 2025 amendment to rule 3 1 d added real safeguards senior officers only, written reasons, exact urls, monthly review . it still says nothing about telling the user. my take: you can't challenge an order you can't see. 1️⃣ write user notice into rule 3 1 d , so it applies across india, not just in one high court's territory 2️⃣ give the user the reasons, with narrow exceptions recorded in writing 3️⃣ where urgency rules out prior notice, give a hearing within a fixed time after the block 4️⃣ publish figures from the monthly reviews 5️⃣ block the item, not the whole page, wherever possible if your page or account is blocked slide 7 : save the platform's message, ask for the order grievance officer, rti , test it against rule 3 1 d , record your losses, and move the high court early. 📎 resources: • p&h hc ruling livelaw : https://lnkd.in/dxen8vg9 • kerala hc on nocap livelaw : https://lnkd.in/dbcvn-5e • 2025 rule 3 1 d amendment nishith desai associates : https://lnkd.in/d5avjtfs should every user get a copy of the order that blocks their content? views are personal; t: Can a privacy law stop journalists from doing their job? India's biggest media houses have asked the Supreme Court.
s: Reuters reported on 26 October that 21 news publishers, acting through the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), have challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. DNPA members…
x: can a privacy law stop journalists from doing their job? india's biggest media houses have asked the supreme court. reuters reported on 26 october that 21 news publishers, acting through the digital news publishers association dnpa , have challenged the digital personal data protection act. dnpa members include network18, ndtv, the indian express and times internet. the case is listed for hearing on 27 october. they want key provisions struck down before they take effect in may 2027. their four concerns: 🔹 notice and consent ss. 5–6 : journalists may need consent from the very people they investigate 🔹 erasure ss. 8 7 , 12 : withdrawal of consent and erasure with no public-interest safeguard could force stories off the record 🔹 information demands s. 36 with rule 23 : the centre can call for information from any data fiduciary, risking exposure of sources 🔹 blocking s. 37 : access can be blocked "in the interests of the general public" underneath it all: there is no exemption for journalism. the 2018 draft, the 2019 bill and the 2021 jpc version all had one. it was dropped in 2022. the state gets wide exemptions under s. 17; the press gets none. the government's position: in july 2025, meity told media bodies no exemption was needed, said journalists aren't data fiduciaries, and offered faqs. separate petitions by venkatesh nayak, the reporters' collective and ncpri on the rti amendment and s. 36 were referred to a larger bench in february 2026, without a stay. today, a journalist's only clear relief is s. 3 c ii : data the person or a legal duty made public falls outside the act. most investigative material doesn't fit. my take: fix it, don't scrap it. 1️⃣ put the exemption in the law; an faq can't override the text 2️⃣ base it on purpose journalism in the public interest , not status, so freelancers are covered 3️⃣ keep security and breach duties; newsrooms hold sensitive data too 4️⃣ require independent or judicial approval before s. 36 demands reach journalistic material 5️⃣ apply a public-interest test before published reports or archives are erased the eu, uk and singapore all build this balance in slide 5 . newsroom checklist on slide 7: subscriber and employee data is covered whatever the court decides. 📎 resources: • reuters report via wtvb : https://lnkd.in/dugfm4bu • sc notice on the earlier petitions the wire : https://lnkd.in/dvqz9bdr • meity–media meeting the tech trace : https://lnkd.in/djkpitie should india's privacy law have a journalism exemption? views are personal; t: The keys that secure the internet are supposed to take billions of years to guess. An AI agent guessed these in one prompt.
s: What happened:
x: the keys that secure the internet are supposed to take billions of years to guess. an ai agent guessed these in one prompt. what happened: emudhra, a licensed indian certificate authority ca , published eight intermediate certificate keys in april 2025. because of a faulty step in its key-generation ceremony, each private key was a number below 256. trying 256 values was enough to recover them. security researcher scott helme said he recovered all eight in under a second, and that an ai agent did the same from a single prompt. the flaw went unnoticed for about 18 months, through two audit cycles. once a researcher reported it on 17 october, mozilla and chrome blocked the certificates the same day, apple and microsoft followed, and emudhra revoked all eight. emudhra says it has found no evidence of misuse, that only one us customer ecosystem was affected, and that its indian digital signature and esign services run on separate systems and are unaffected. why lawyers should care: a ca is a digital notary. whoever holds its private key can forge trusted certificates, impersonate websites and intercept encrypted traffic. what the it act says chapter vi : 🔹 section 30: a ca must use hardware, software and procedures secure from intrusion and misuse 🔹 section 34 2 : if an event affects the integrity of its systems, it must use reasonable efforts to notify those likely to be affected 🔹 section 25: the controller of certifying authorities cca can suspend or revoke a licence for failing to maintain section 30 procedures the questions this raises my take : 1️⃣ two regimes: the it act licenses cas for electronic signature certificates; website certificates are policed mainly by browser root programs. do section 30 duties reach a licensed ca's global tls business? that's untested. 2️⃣ the weak keys passed two audits. what were the auditors checking? 3️⃣ who compensates relying parties? section 43a covers only sensitive personal data, and dpdp security duties start in may 2027. for now, remedies sit mostly in contracts and their liability caps. the contrast is striking: four foreign browser makers acted within 72 hours. as of 21 october, the cca had made no public statement, though meity officials said a team was investigating. 📎 resources: • medianama explainer: https://lnkd.in/durty7wz • bleepingcomputer: https://lnkd.in/dxpzpe8c • emudhra's statement: https://lnkd.in/dkc dn84 should india's ca rules be rewritten for the ai era? exist. what the draft requires: 1️⃣ disclosure in every filing every submission must carry a declaration annexure i stating whether ai was used. if it was, you confirm that every citation, rule and fact was independently verified. not disclosing is treated as misrepresentation. 2️⃣ a 4-point citation test before citing any case, confirm that: • it exists and was decided by the court named • the citation details are correct • the holding attributed to it is accurate • it is relevant and read the full judgment from a non-ai source: court websites, the gazette, scc online, manupatra. 3️⃣ no ai-made evidence ai cannot change the substance of affidavits, or fabricate or alter labels, invoices, sales data, surveys, website extracts, translations or proof of use. if authenticity is doubted, the registrar can demand the native file, metadata, audit trails and server logs, and draw adverse inferences. 4️⃣ real consequences after a show-cause notice and hearing, the registrar can strike out the citation or the whole submission. agents can be sent to a disciplinary committee and advocates to the bar council. anyone can report a suspected fake citation annexure ii , but frivolous reports can be penalised too. the principle running through it: "final decision-making authority … shall rest at all times with the submitting human." using ai is no defence. why it matters: courts have been sanctioning fake ai citations case by case. this is one of the first times an indian regulator has written down rules for people who appear before it. the patent office issued ai guidelines for its t: Should children be kept off the internet to keep them safe? The Supreme Court has said no.
s: In Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish (order dated 15 October 2026, Pardiwala & Chandran, JJ.), the Court held that internet access is a fundamental right for every individual…
x: should children be kept off the internet to keep them safe? the supreme court has said no. in just rights for children alliance v. s. harish order dated 15 october 2026, pardiwala & chandran, jj. , the court held that internet access is a fundamental right for every individual, children included, under article 21 read with article 19 1 a . its reasoning in one line: "to keep the child away from the internet on account of such failures would be to mistake the victim for the problem." key holdings: 🔹 blanket, age-based bans are disproportionate. they may push children to unregulated platforms and make them less likely to report abuse 🔹 checking every user's age carries its own risk of sensitive data collection and surveillance 🔹 protection should target the harm: those who make, share or sell child sexual exploitation and abuse material cseam , and platforms that fail to remove it 🔹 platforms that ignore pocso and it rules duties cannot rely on safe harbour under section 79 what the court wants instead: ✔ a "child mode": private by default, limited contact from unknown adults, moderated ads and content ✔ a national hash & url list database for cseam, with at least three trained human analysts making the final assessment ✔ immediate removal of content that matches the database ✔ reporting within two steps, acknowledgement within 24 hours, and final decisions by trained humans, not algorithms ✔ exemplary fines scaled to a platform's size and turnover, and forfeiture of revenue earned from such content behind paywalls ✔ digital safety education in schools and free counselling for victims the centre must report progress by the next hearing on 10 december 2026. my take: the dpdp angle slide 7 section 9 of the dpdp act requires verifiable parental consent before processing data of anyone under 18, and bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted ads aimed at children, from 13 may 2027. but verifying consent means knowing who is a child, and the court has warned that checking everyone's age is itself a privacy risk. platforms will need age checks that collect as little data as possible. the burden has shifted from children to platforms. 📎 t: Your account or page was blocked. What can you do?
s: A step-by-step guide for Indian users, creators and businesses whose Instagram, Facebook, X or YouTube account or post has been blocked: who blocked it, how to appeal, and when courts can help.
x: in short - first work out who blocked you. a block by the platform and a block ordered by the government have different remedies. - platform block: appeal in the app, then complain to the platform's grievance officer, then appeal to the grievance appellate committee gac within 30 days. after that, a civil suit. - government block: ask for the order, and challenge it in the high court by writ petition. - save everything from day one. screenshots, emails, dates and your losses are your evidence at every stage. step 1: save the evidence before you do anything else: 1. screenshot the block or suspension message, with the date and time visible. 2. save every email or in-app notice the platform sends you. 3. note your account name, url, follower count and, if you earn from the account, what you're losing each week. 4. if you can still log in, download your data most platforms have a "download your information" option . step 2: who blocked you? who blocked it usual signs main route --- --- --- the platform itself message says it broke "community standards", spam, impersonation or a copyright complaint in-app appeal → grievance officer → gac → civil suit the government message says "withheld in india", "in response to a legal demand" or a government notice ask for the order → writ petition in the high court the problem is that platform messages often don't say which it is. if you can't tell, ask the platform's grievance officer directly, in writing: was this action taken under your own policies, or on a government order or notice? if the platform blocked you 1. appeal inside the app straight away. use the "request review" or "appeal" option. keep the reference number. 2. complain to the grievance officer. every platform must publish a grievance officer's contact details usually in its help centre or legal pages . under the it rules, 2021, the grievance officer has to acknowledge your complaint within 24 hours and resolve it within 15 days. 3. appeal to the grievance appellate committee. if the grievance officer rejects you or doesn't reply, appeal online at gac.gov.in . you can appeal within 30 days of the grievance officer's decision, or of getting no response. the gac is meant to try to decide appeals within 30 days. in practice it is badly backlogged: as of 22 september 2026, 49,978 of 63,353 appeals were pending. 4. use your right to reasons. large platforms significant social media intermediaries must, under rule 4 8 of the it rules, notify you with reasons and give you a fair chance to dispute when they remove content or disable access on their own. quote rule 4 8 in your complaints. 5. civil suit, if needed. if none of this works, the remedy is a civil suit for restoration and damages if you can prove loss . you can't usually go straight to the high court by writ against the platform: in sarthak bhagat v. union of india 27 october 2026 , the delhi high court held that meta doesn't perform a public function, so a writ isn't maintainable against it. can the platform make you sue in california? not necessarily. in meta platforms v. blink digital 27 october 2026 , the bombay high court refused to send an indian advertiser's suit to california despite meta's terms, because it raised duties under the it act and it rules that an indian court has to decide. if it was a copyright complaint platforms may act on copyright complaints, and can suspend accounts. in anmol jain v. union of india 17 september 2026 , the madhya pradesh high court upheld this, treating the grievance officer and gac as adequate safeguards. but you can still: - ask for the complaint itself: who claimed it, and which work they say you copied; - argue fair dealing memes, commentary and reviews may qualify under section 52 of the copyright act ; - under the copyright rules, 2013 rule 75 , the complainant has to identify the work and their ownership, and if no court order follows within 21 days the content may be restored. if the government ordered the block there are two main legal routes the government uses: - section 69a of the it act with the 2009 blocking rules. these give the originator notice and a hearing where possible. - section 79 3 b notices to the platform. since the 2025 amendment to rule 3 1 d , these can only be issued by senior, specifically authorised officers at least dig rank for police , in writing, with reasons and exact urls. what to do: 1. ask for the order. write to the platform's grievance officer asking for a copy of the government order or notice, and who issued it. you can also file an rti application with the department you suspect. 2. check it. was it issued by an officer with power to issue it? does it give reasons? does it name specific posts, or the whole page? 3. go to the high court. a government block can be challenged by writ petition. in haryana 24 news network v. union of india reported 20 october 2026 , the punjab & haryana high court held that a notice issued by a superintendent of police was without jurisdiction, that a copy must go to the user too, and ordered the page restored within 24 hours. checklist - screenshots of the block notice, with date and time - in-app appeal filed; reference number saved - written complaint to the grievance officer; date noted - gac appeal filed within 30 days calendar reminder set - written request asking whether a government order was involved - record of lost income or business - backup of your content and followers list common questions can i complain to the police? only if a crime is involved, for example if someone hacked your account or is impersonating you. a platform's policy decision isn't a police matter. will a lawyer's notice help? sometimes. a notice citing rule 4 8 and asking for reasons and restoration can prompt a review, and it is useful evidence if you later sue. my account was hacked, not blocked. that's different: use the platform's hacked-account recovery process, and report the hacking at cybercrime.gov.in or on 1930.

t: Got a "digital arrest" call? What to do, step by step
s: How to recognise a digital arrest scam, what to do during the call, how to report it, and what to do in the first hours if you have already paid, including your rights against your bank.
x: in short - there is no such thing as a "digital arrest". no police, cbi, ed, customs, rbi or court officer arrests anyone over a video call, keeps them "under watch" on camera, or asks for money to "verify" or "clear" their name. - hang up. don't share details, don't install apps, don't transfer money. - already paid? call 1930 immediately. the faster you report, the better the chance of freezing the money. - tell your parents and grandparents. older people are the most frequent targets. how the scam works a caller claims to be from the police, cbi, ed, customs, a courier company or trai. they say a parcel in your name had drugs, your aadhaar was used for money laundering, or your number is linked to a crime. they move you to a video call, sometimes with someone in uniform and a fake police station or courtroom behind them. they may show "arrest warrants" or court orders with seals, which are forged. then they tell you: - you are under "digital arrest" and must stay on camera; - you must not tell anyone, or you'll be arrested; - to prove your innocence, you must transfer your savings to a "safe" or "rbi-verified" account, to be returned after "verification". the money never comes back. red flags - any official asking you to stay on a video call "under arrest" - any official asking you to transfer money to "verify" or "secure" it - pressure to keep it secret , even from family - warrants, notices or court orders sent on whatsapp - calls from unknown numbers, sometimes with a +91 number that looks official - threats that get louder the more questions you ask if the call is happening now 1. disconnect. you have no legal duty to stay on the call. 2. don't send money, otps, aadhaar, pan or bank details. don't install any app they ask for screen-sharing apps let them see everything . 3. talk to someone you trust immediately, a family member or friend. the secrecy is part of the scam. 4. if you're genuinely worried , call your local police station yourself, using a number you look up independently. never use a number the caller gives you. if you haven't lost money: report the call report the number, whatsapp account or message on chakshu , the fraud-reporting facility on the department of telecommunications' sanchar saathi portal sancharsaathi.gov.in, or the sanchar saathi app . this helps block the numbers so others aren't targeted. if you've already paid: the first hours matter do these in order, as fast as you can: 1. call 1930 , the national cyber fraud helpline. give your phone number, the amount, your bank, the time of each transfer, and the receiving account or upi id. 2. file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in under "financial fraud". upload screenshots, call logs, transaction receipts and any fake documents. note the complaint number. 3. tell your bank in writing , by email and at the branch, asking it to block further transactions and to request a hold on the receiving accounts. keep the acknowledgement. 4. file an fir at your local police station or cyber police station, quoting your cybercrime.gov.in complaint number. 5. escalate if the bank doesn't help: complain to the bank's grievance officer, and after 30 days, or if the reply is unsatisfactory, to the rbi ombudsman at cms.rbi.org.in. keep everything: call logs, chat screenshots, the "documents" they sent, bank smses and statements. don't delete the chats. will the bank refund your money? until recently, often not. the rbi's 2017 rules limit your liability for unauthorised electronic transactions where the bank is at fault. but in a digital arrest, you make the transfer yourself, under fear, so banks have treated it as authorised , even when sudden, unusual transfers went through without a single check. that is changing. in the supreme court's suo motu case on digital arrest scams, a bench led by the chief justice said on 29 october 2026 that the rbi's new rules must include a liability clause: banks must compensate victims where inadequate safeguards or a failure of due diligence contributed to the fraud, for not less than the amount lost. the court also asked whatsapp to propose measures against these scams. the rbi's new rules are expected by the end of 2026, and the case is next listed on 23 november 2026. what this means for you now: in your complaint to the bank and the rbi ombudsman, point out any warning signs the bank ignored, for example a large first-time transfer to a new payee, several transfers in a short time, or a transfer that emptied a long-held fixed deposit or savings account. protect your family - tell older relatives, clearly: no officer arrests anyone on a video call, and no officer asks for money. - agree a family rule: anyone who gets such a call phones a family member before doing anything. - set lower daily transfer limits on bank and upi accounts for elderly relatives, and turn on transaction alerts. - save 1930 in everyone's phone. common questions what if they really are police? real police don't question or arrest people over video calls, and never ask for money transfers. if you're served a genuine notice, it comes through proper channels and you can verify it with the police station or court directly. i paid days ago. is it too late? report anyway, immediately. recovery is harder after a delay, but the complaint is still needed for the investigation and for any claim against the bank. should i pay someone who promises to "recover" my money? no. t: Is your neighbour's CCTV camera legal? Your rights, and the rules for installing one
s: What Indian courts say about private CCTV cameras pointed at a neighbour's home, what you can do if a camera invades your privacy, and how to install your own camera lawfully.
x: in short - you can install cctv to protect your own home. that's lawful. - but it can't be positioned to intrude on your neighbour's privacy, for example by watching their front door, windows or courtyard. - courts balance it case by case: where the camera points, what it records, why it's there, and what's done with the footage. - if a camera faces your home: talk, then write, then approach the district magistrate, a civil court, or the police if private moments are recorded or shared. what the courts have said - allahabad high court 2026 . in yogendra maurya v. state of u.p. order dated 26 october 2026 , the court said no private cctv camera can be installed and positioned in a way that interferes with a neighbour's privacy. it directed the district magistrate to decide the petitioner's complaint within a month. - kerala high court 2023 . security can't be a pretext to snoop on neighbours. the court asked the state police chief to frame cctv guidelines. - calcutta high court, upheld by the supreme court 2025 . cameras inside a shared house need the consent of all occupants. - kerala high court 2025 . a camera protecting an elderly woman facing real threats was allowed to stay. genuine safety needs count. which law applies? - the constitution. privacy is a fundamental right under article 21 k.s. puttaswamy , 2017 , and courts apply that principle in disputes between neighbours. - the dpdp act doesn't cover a household camera. section 3 c i excludes personal data processed for personal or domestic purposes. but cameras run by housing societies rwas , shops and offices are a different matter, and from may 2027 they will have duties under the act. - criminal law, for the serious cases. capturing or sharing images of a person's private area without consent is an offence under section 66e of the it act. voyeurism and intruding on a woman's privacy are offences under sections 77 and 79 of the bharatiya nyaya sanhita. - civil law. a civil court can order a camera to be moved, masked or removed. if a neighbour's camera faces your home 1. gather facts quietly. take photos showing the camera's position and angle relative to your door or windows. note when it was installed. 2. talk first. many disputes end when the owner learns about privacy masking or simply turns the camera. 3. write a polite letter asking them to reposition or mask the camera within a reasonable time. keep a copy and proof of delivery. 4. approach the authorities if it continues: - the district magistrate , especially where it's a public-nuisance or law-and-order concern; - a civil court , for an order to move or remove the camera; - the police , if private acts are recorded, or footage is shared or used to harass. 5. your housing society may help if the camera is in a common area. don't damage, cover or remove the camera yourself. that can expose you to a complaint. if you're installing a camera - point it at your own property: your gate, door and parking, not the neighbour's. - use privacy masking. most cameras let you black out parts of the frame. - skip audio. recording conversations is far more intrusive than video. - secure the footage: a strong password, two-factor login on the app, and no default passwords. - auto-delete after a short period unless there's an incident. - never post other people's footage online to shame or expose them. - in a shared house or building, get everyone's consent for cameras inside common spaces. - put up a small notice saying cctv is in use. it's courteous, and deters intruders. for housing societies, shops and offices from 13 may 2027, most duties under the dpdp act will apply to you as a data fiduciary: a clear notice that cctv is in use and why, reasonable security for the footage, limited retention, access only for authorised people, and a way for residents or customers to raise concerns. it's sensible to set this up now. common questions my neighbour says it's for security. does that settle it? no. security is a legitimate reason, but the camera still has to be positioned so it doesn't intrude more than necessary. can i ask to see what their camera records? you can ask, and showing you the view often resolves the dispute. if they refuse, that can be something to raise with the district magistrate or a court. is a doorbell camera different? it's judged the same way: by what it captures. a doorbell camera that only covers your own doorstep is very different from one that looks straight into a neighbour's flat.

t: DPDP Act: what your business must do by 13 May 2027
s: A plain-language checklist for Indian businesses, startups, schools and apps on the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules, 2025, with the key dates, duties and penalties.
x: in short - most duties start on 13 may 2027. that's when notice, consent, security, breach reporting, retention and children's data rules all take effect. - they apply whether or not the data protection board is ready. as of mid-november 2026, no board chairperson or member has been appointed, but the deadline hasn't moved. - penalties go up to ₹250 crore per breach, so this is a board-level issue, not just an it task. - start with a data map. you can't comply with rules about data you haven't found. the timeline date what happens --- --- 13 november 2025 dpdp rules notified. the data protection board established in law. 13 november 2026 consent manager registration opens s. 6 9 , rule 4 . 13 may 2027 almost everything else: notices, consent, security safeguards, breach reporting, retention and erasure, children's data, significant data fiduciary duties, and users' rights. does it apply to you? yes, if you process digital personal data in india: customer, employee, student, patient or user data held on computers, apps, websites or cloud services, or paper data that you digitise. it also applies to businesses outside india that offer goods or services to people in india. two important exclusions: - personal or domestic use s. 3 c i , for example a family's own cctv or phone contacts. - data the person has made public themselves , or that is published under a legal duty s. 3 c ii . in the act's terms, you're a data fiduciary if you decide why and how data is processed. vendors who process data for you are data processors , and you remain responsible for them. your checklist 1. map your data start now list every place you collect or hold personal data: website forms, apps, crm, hr and payroll, cctv, email marketing lists, whatsapp groups, spreadsheets, and every vendor that receives data. for each, note what data, why you collect it, who can access it, where it's stored, how long you keep it, and whether it leaves india. flag children's data and data of persons with disability. they need extra steps see 6 below . 2. rewrite your privacy notice before or when you ask for consent, your notice must be clear and stand on its own. it should list, item by item, the personal data you collect and the specific purpose for each, and explain how people can withdraw consent, exercise their rights and complain to the board. people must be able to read it in english or any language in the eighth schedule of the constitution. 3. fix consent, and make withdrawal easy - consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear action. no pre-ticked boxes. - withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it. if someone gives consent in one click, they should be able to withdraw it in one click. - where you rely on a "legitimate use" instead of consent for example, for employment purposes , document why. 4. put security safeguards in place reasonable safeguards include encryption or masking of personal data, access controls, logs of who accessed what, and backups. keep access logs and related data for at least one year so breaches can be detected and investigated. write these duties into your vendor contracts too. 5. prepare a breach playbook when you become aware of a personal data breach, you must tell each affected person and the data protection board without delay, and send the board a detailed report within 72 hours rule 7 . that's only possible if you've decided in advance: - who leads the response, and who can approve notifications; - how you'll reach affected users email, sms, in-app ; - templates for the user notice and the board report. 6. children and persons with disability - before processing a child's data anyone under 18 , you need verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian . the same applies to a person with disability who has a lawful guardian. - you must not track, monitor the behaviour of, or target ads at children. - verifying age shouldn't mean collecting more data than you need. the supreme court has warned that checking everyone's age is itself a privacy risk, so choose methods that collect as little as possible. this matters most for ed-tech, schools, coaching institutes, gaming, health and social apps. 7. retention and erasure delete personal data once the purpose is served or consent is withdrawn, unless a law requires you to keep it. large e-commerce, online gaming and social media platforms above the user thresholds in the third schedule must erase a user's data after three years of inactivity , after telling them at least 48 hours in advance. 8. respond to users' rights people can ask to access a summary of their data, correct it, complete it, erase it, and nominate someone to act for them. publish contact details of a person who can answer questions about your data processing a data protection officer if you're a significant data fiduciary , and set up a grievance process with a response timeline. 9. significant data fiduciaries if the government notifies you as a significant data fiduciary based on the volume and sensitivity of data you process , you'll also need a data protection officer based in india, an independent data auditor, periodic data protection impact assessments, and a periodic data audit. penalties the schedule to the act sets maximum penalties per instance: failure up to --- --- reasonable security safeguards to prevent a breach ₹250 crore notifying a breach to the board and affected users ₹200 crore children's data duties ₹200 crore significant data fiduciary duties ₹150 crore other breaches of the act or rules ₹50 crore a six-month plan now to february 2027 - map your data and flag children's data - add data-processing clauses to every vendor contract - draft your new privacy notice and consent text march to may 2027 - build one-click consent withdrawal - put encryption, access controls and logging in place - set up your 72-hour breach playbook and run a mock drill - publish a contact person and a grievance process common questions we're a small business. does this apply to us? yes. there's no general exemption for small businesses, though the government can notify exemptions for certain classes, such as startups. check the gazette before relying on one. the board has no members. can we wait? no. the legal duties start on 13 may 2027 regardless, and high courts have already been directing people to the board. waiting only leaves you exposed once it is staffed. do we need a consent manager? no. consent managers are registered platforms people can use to manage consent across many businesses. you may need to work with them, but you don't have to become one.
